nameStory: Flowering spurge gets its name from its showy display of small white flowers that bloom throughout the summer, making it stand out among its spurge relatives. The word 'spurge' comes from an old French word meaning 'to purge,' referring to the traditional medicinal use of plants in this family as laxatives.
description: Flowering spurge is a tall, upright wildflower that can reach up to 3 feet high, making it one of the most impressive spurges you'll encounter. Unlike many of its low-growing relatives, this perennial stands proud with smooth green stems topped by clusters of tiny white flowers. The light green leaves are arranged alternately up the stem or sometimes in small whorls, giving the plant a neat, organized appearance. It blooms reliably from June through September, creating patches of white in sunny meadows and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters at stem tips, each flower only about 1/4 inch across with five white bracts that look like petals but aren't true petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright, reaching 2-3 feet high with smooth, unbranched stems that feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Light green, narrow leaves about 3 inches long and 1/2 inch wide, arranged alternately or in whorls, with smooth edges and a slightly thick texture

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Milky white sap oozes from broken stems or leaves - be careful not to get it on your skin or in your eyes as it can cause irritation

habitat: Flowering spurge thrives in sunny, well-drained locations like meadows, prairies, roadsides, and field edges throughout New England. It prefers sandy or gravelly soils and is often found in disturbed areas where other tall wildflowers grow. You'll typically spot it in open areas with full sun exposure, rarely in shaded woodlands.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from underground roots, growing rapidly into tall stems with fresh light green leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through September, with clusters of small white flowers creating an impressive display that attracts many pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small seed capsules develop, while leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only underground roots to survive until spring regrowth.

funFact: Despite looking like innocent white flowers, flowering spurge is actually showing off fake petals - what appear to be five white petals are really specialized leaves called bracts, while the true flowers are tiny green structures in the center that most people never notice!
confusionNotes: Flowering spurge is sometimes mistaken for Queen Anne's lace or other white-flowered plants, but its milky sap and the arrangement of leaves up the stem are dead giveaways - Queen Anne's lace has feathery leaves and clear sap.
contextualKnowledge: All spurges produce a milky latex sap that has been used medicinally for centuries, but modern gardeners and nature lovers should be cautious as this sap can cause skin irritation, eye problems, and is toxic if ingested - always wash hands after handling any spurge plant.
compareHints: Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge. While other spurges have small, inconspicuous flowers, flowering spurge puts on a real show with its white flower clusters. Its upright growth habit and larger size make it easily distinguishable from the creeping or prostrate growth of most other local spurges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
